questions.question: Design a real-time leaderboard for a gaming platform with 10 million users.
questions.title: Design a Real-Time Gaming Leaderboard
questions.direct_answer: Use **Redis Sorted Sets** as the leaderboard primitive — `ZADD` updates a score atomically; `ZRANK` and `ZREVRANGE` give rank/range in **O(log N)**. Layer the design as: **Game Service** publishes score events to **Kafka**; a **Score Aggregator** writes to per-leaderboard ZSETs in Redis (global, regional, friend-group, time-windowed). Cache the **top-N** in CDN/edge for the public view; serve **rank-of-self + nearby slice** from Redis for personalized views. **Persist scores to a durable store** (Postgres/Cassandra) for replay and recovery, and **rebuild Redis from there** on cold start.

interviewer_intent.testing: Choosing the right data structure (Redis sorted sets), partitioning leaderboards by scope and time, durability vs in-memory trade-offs, and handling tie-breaking + cheating.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relational `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT N` for rank-of-self (O(N) count of higher scores), or treating Redis as the source of truth with no durable backstop.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss partitioned leaderboards (global/regional/friends), time-windowed (daily/weekly/all-time) with separate ZSETs, anti-cheat verification before publish, and cold-start rebuild strategy.

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
A leaderboard answers two distinct questions, both fast:

- **"Top N players"** — read-mostly, broadcast to millions of viewers.
- **"What rank am I, and who's near me?"** — personalized, computed per-user.

The SQL approach (`ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT N`) handles the first acceptably until score updates flood in. The second — "my rank" — becomes O(N) (`SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE score > my_score`). At 10M users and 10K score updates/sec, this is the wrong shape.

Why this isn't a solved problem just by "use Redis":

- **Partitioning** — there isn't one leaderboard. There's global, regional, country, friend-group, daily, weekly, all-time, season-X. Each is its own ranked structure.
- **Tie-breaking** — two players score 9999. Rank is ambiguous unless we encode tiebreakers into the sort key.
- **Anti-cheat** — score updates come from clients. We can't trust them; need server-side validation.
- **Durability** — Redis is in-memory; a restart loses state if we trust it as source-of-truth.
- **Hot global leaderboard reads** — "top 100 globally" is the most-viewed page on the site; it'd melt one Redis shard without caching.
- **Score arrival rate** during peak (tournament finals) can spike to 100K updates/sec on a single leaderboard.

The central architectural decision: **Redis Sorted Sets for the hot path**, **Kafka + durable store for the write path with replay**, **CDN cache for public read views**, and **partitioned ZSETs by leaderboard scope** so writes don't fan out across one giant key.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- **Score semantics** — monotonically increasing (XP), or arbitrary (latest match score)?
- **Leaderboard scopes** — global only, or regional / country / friend-group?
- **Time windows** — all-time, season, weekly, daily?
- **Tie-breaking rule** — first-to-reach-score wins, or random?
- **Personalized view** — "my rank + 10 above + 10 below"?
- **Score archive** — historical replay for past seasons?

**Non-functional**
- **Score update rate** — average and peak (tournament finals)?
- **Read traffic** for top-N (cached) vs personalized (per-user)?
- **Latency budget** — sub-100 ms for score update, sub-50 ms for read.
- **Anti-cheat** — server-validated scores or client-trusted?
- **Multi-region** — one global leaderboard or per-region with global aggregation?

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **10M total users**, **1M DAU**, **100K concurrent during peak events**.
- **Score updates**: ~5K/sec average, 100K/sec during tournament finals.
- **Read traffic**: ~50K/sec for top-N (mostly cached), ~20K/sec for personalized ("my rank + nearby").
- **Leaderboards in scope**: global all-time, global daily, global weekly, regional all-time (10 regions), friend-group (per-user, computed on the fly).
- **Tie-breaking**: encode `(score * 1e9) - timestamp_ms` so earlier-reach wins.
- **Anti-cheat**: server-side validation — score updates only from authoritative match-result service.
- **Sub-100 ms p99 for score update**, sub-50 ms p99 for read.
- **Durability**: scores persisted to Cassandra; Redis can be rebuilt from there.
- **Multi-region**: per-region writes locally; global leaderboard maintained by cross-region async merge.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- 100K writes/sec at peak across all leaderboards.
- Per leaderboard, the global all-time gets the most writes (~30K/sec at peak).
- Single Redis instance handles ~80K ZADD/sec; sharded cluster scales horizontally by leaderboard key.

**Storage**

- Per ZSET entry: user_id (8 bytes) + score (8 bytes) + skip-list overhead (~50 bytes) = ~70 bytes.
- Global all-time ZSET: 10M users × 70 bytes ≈ **700 MB Redis**.
- All scopes combined: ~5 GB Redis (global + 10 regional + 7 daily windows + 4 weekly windows).
- Cassandra durable store: 10M users × multiple leaderboards × ~100 bytes/row = **a few GB**, trivial.
- Daily score event log: 5K/sec × 86,400 × ~200 bytes/event = **~85 GB/day** — archived to S3 weekly.

**Latency budget**

- Score validation: 5 ms
- Kafka publish: 2 ms
- ZADD across N ZSETs (global + regional + windowed): N × 1 ms ≈ 5 ms
- Cassandra write: 5 ms async
- Total perceived: ~15 ms — well under 100 ms budget.

**Read latency**

- ZREVRANGE top-100: 0.5 ms.
- ZREVRANK my rank: 0.5 ms.
- ZREVRANGEBYSCORE for nearby slice: 1 ms.
- Total personalized read: ~5 ms server-side.

**Conclusion**: bottleneck is hot-leaderboard writes during tournament; sharding by leaderboard key handles it.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
**Submit a score:**

```http
POST /api/v1/scores
Authorization: Bearer ...    (server-to-server only)
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "user_id": "u_99",
  "score": 9876,
  "match_id": "m_abc",
  "region": "us-west",
  "occurred_at": "2026-04-21T10:00:00.123Z"
}

202 Accepted
{
  "event_id": "evt_7Z3kY8"
}
```

Returned `202` because actual leaderboard update is async (ms behind).

**Read top-N:**

```http
GET /api/v1/leaderboards/{board}/top?limit=100
     where board = global-all-time | global-daily | regional-us-west | etc.

200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=10

{
  "board": "global-all-time",
  "updated_at": "...",
  "entries": [
    {"rank": 1, "user_id": "u_42", "display_name": "...", "score": 99999},
    ...
  ]
}
```

**My rank + nearby slice:**

```http
GET /api/v1/leaderboards/{board}/rank/{user_id}?neighbors=10

200 OK
{
  "user_id": "u_99",
  "rank": 4521,
  "score": 9876,
  "nearby": [
    {"rank":4511, "user_id":"...", "score":9890},
    ...,
    {"rank":4531, "user_id":"...", "score":9860}
  ]
}
```

**Friend-group leaderboard** (computed at request time):

```http
GET /api/v1/leaderboards/friends/{user_id}
```

sections.title: Data Model and Sorted-Set Layout
sections.content:
**Redis sorted sets — one ZSET per (board_id, time_window)**:

```
KEY:    lb:global:all-time             # one giant board
KEY:    lb:global:daily:2026-04-21     # daily reset
KEY:    lb:global:weekly:2026-W17      # weekly reset
KEY:    lb:regional:us-west:all-time   # regional
KEY:    lb:regional:eu-west:all-time
KEY:    lb:season:5:all-time           # per-season

MEMBER: user_id
SCORE:  encoded_score (see tie-breaking)
```

**Tie-breaking via score encoding** — floating-point score is 64-bit double; we encode:

```
encoded_score = score * 1e9 - (timestamp_ms - epoch)
```

Higher encoded_score wins; for equal raw scores, the earlier-reach time has higher encoded_score.

**Display name and metadata** stored separately:

```
KEY:  user:{user_id}
TYPE: HASH
FIELDS: display_name, avatar_url, country, last_active
```

**Durable store (Cassandra)**:

```cql
CREATE TABLE score_events (
    event_id   timeuuid,
    user_id    text,
    board_id   text,
    score      bigint,
    match_id   text,
    occurred_at timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((board_id), occurred_at, event_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (occurred_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE current_scores (
    user_id    text,
    board_id   text,
    score      bigint,
    updated_at timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, board_id))
);
```

`score_events` is append-only audit; `current_scores` is the latest value per user-board, used to rebuild Redis on cold start.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ SCORE_EVENTS : produces
    USERS ||--o{ CURRENT_SCORES : has
    LEADERBOARDS ||--o{ SCORE_EVENTS : aggregates
    LEADERBOARDS ||--o{ CURRENT_SCORES : ranks
    USERS {
        text user_id PK
        text display_name
        text country
    }
    LEADERBOARDS {
        text board_id PK
        text scope
        text time_window
    }
    SCORE_EVENTS {
        text board_id FK
        timeuuid event_id PK
        text user_id FK
        bigint score
        text match_id
    }
    CURRENT_SCORES {
        text user_id FK
        text board_id FK
        bigint score
        timestamp updated_at
    }
```

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
Three logical paths: **submit** (write through Kafka), **aggregate** (Redis ZSETs + Cassandra), **read** (cached top-N + per-user). ```mermaid flowchart TB Client([Game Client]) GameSvc[Game Service
match validator] AntiCheat[Anti-Cheat] Kafka{{Kafka
scores.submitted}} Aggregator[Score Aggregator
writes to all relevant ZSETs] Redis[(Redis Cluster
per-leaderboard ZSETs)] Cassandra[(Cassandra
durable scores + events)] LBApi[Leaderboard API] CDN[CDN
top-N cache] UserApp([Players]) Client --> GameSvc GameSvc --> AntiCheat AntiCheat -->|valid| Kafka Kafka --> Aggregator Aggregator --> Redis Aggregator --> Cassandra UserApp -->|GET top| CDN CDN -.miss.-> LBApi LBApi --> Redis UserApp -->|GET my-rank| LBApi classDef edge fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 classDef svc fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e classDef store fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef bus fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b class CDN,LBApi edge class GameSvc,AntiCheat,Aggregator svc class Redis,Cassandra store class Kafka bus ``` **Submit path:** match ends → Game Service computes score → Anti-Cheat validates → publishes to Kafka. Score Aggregator consumes; for each board the user belongs to (global, regional, daily window, etc.), executes `ZADD`. Also writes to Cassandra for durability. **Read path:** top-N requests hit CDN with 10s TTL; on miss, served from Redis. Personalized requests bypass CDN (per-user, not cacheable globally) and hit Redis directly.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design
Partitioned and Time-Windowed Leaderboards
sections.content:
**Partition by scope** — don't put everything in one giant ZSET.

- `lb:global:all-time` — one big ZSET, sharded by Redis Cluster.
- `lb:regional:us-west:all-time` — smaller, lower contention.
- `lb:country:in:all-time`, `lb:country:us:all-time`, etc.
- `lb:season:7:all-time` — per-season; resets every season.

**Time-windowed boards** — separate ZSET per window:

- `lb:global:daily:2026-04-21` — today's leaderboard.
- At midnight UTC, the daily ZSET rolls over; old daily ZSET set with 30-day TTL for historical view.
- Same pattern for weekly: `lb:global:weekly:2026-W17`.
- `BoardResolver` adds the current daily/weekly key to the write fan-out automatically.

**Friend-group leaderboard** — computed on the fly:

```
1. Look up user's friend list (from Social Service).
2. ZMSCORE lb:global:all-time friend1 friend2 ... (batch fetch their scores)
3. Sort in-memory, return top N.
```

Cheap enough for typical friend lists (~150 friends). For very large friend graphs, pre-materialize the friend leaderboard in its own ZSET (`lb:friends:{user_id}`) and update incrementally on friend score change.

**Why partition** — a single ZSET with 10M members is fine for read; the write hot-spot would be one Redis shard taking all 100K updates/sec at peak. Partitioning spreads that across 10+ shards.

sections.title: Anti-Cheat, Hot Reads, and CDN Strategy
sections.content:
**Anti-cheat — never trust the client**:

- Score submission only accepted from the authoritative Game Service (server-to-server auth).
- Game Service validates match outcome (replay, server simulation).
- Anti-Cheat module checks: implausible score growth (impossible per-game gains), known cheating signatures, IP/device anomalies.
- Suspicious scores quarantined; not added to leaderboard until manual review.

**Top-N is the most-viewed page** — CDN absorbs it:

- `Cache-Control: public, max-age=10`.
- 10-second freshness is acceptable for a public ranking; the data churns but the top is stable.
- CDN absorbs ~95% of top-N traffic — origin sees a fraction.
- For high-stakes events (tournament finals), TTL drops to 1 second.

**Per-user reads bypass CDN** (private, per-user; not cacheable across users).

**Hot key on a single board** — `lb:global:all-time` could see hot writes during a tournament. Solution: shard by user_id hash within the board (`lb:global:all-time:0`, `lb:global:all-time:1`, ...) and merge on read. Adds complexity; only needed if a single ZSET becomes the bottleneck.

**Negative caching** — "my rank" for unranked users (never played) cached briefly to avoid hammering Redis with default-rank lookups.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**Redis cluster outage**

- Reads serve from CDN (top-N) for the cache TTL; personalized reads return `503` briefly.
- Writes buffer in Kafka.
- After Redis recovery: the CacheWarmer reads `current_scores` from Cassandra and rebuilds each ZSET. Takes ~2 minutes for the full set; users see stale ranks during.

**Kafka outage**

- Score Submission Service buffers locally (bounded queue).
- After overflow, returns `503` to upstream Game Service; Game Service retries with backoff.
- Once Kafka recovers, backlog drains; aggregator catches up.

**Cassandra outage**

- Aggregator continues writing to Redis (live leaderboard stays correct).
- Cassandra writes accumulate in a Kafka retry topic.
- After recovery, retry topic drains; durable store catches up.
- Risk window: if both Redis AND Cassandra fail simultaneously, latest scores in flight are lost. Multi-region replication mitigates.

**Aggregator crash mid-fanout**

- Kafka offset uncommitted; another instance picks up the same event.
- ZADD with same score is a no-op (idempotent).
- Cassandra upsert is idempotent on event_id.
- Worst case: brief duplicate work; no data corruption.

**Score replay attack** (cheater retries an old high score)

- Anti-Cheat validates `match_id` is unique and recent.
- Score events with stale `occurred_at` (> 1 hour old) rejected unless flagged as legitimate replay.

**Tournament burst (10× normal traffic)**

- Pre-scaled Redis cluster and aggregator workers ahead of scheduled events.
- Per-board Kafka partition count adjusted to allow more parallel consumers.
- Lowered CDN TTL on tournament boards (1s instead of 10s) for fresher viewing.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `score.submit.total{board, status}` — throughput by leaderboard.
- `score.update.latency` p99 — SLO < 100 ms.
- `leaderboard.read.latency{type=top|rank|nearby}` p99 — SLO < 50 ms.
- `cdn.hit_ratio{board=top}` — alert if drops below 80%.
- `anti_cheat.rejection_rate` — spike indicates active cheating attempt.
- `kafka.lag.scores_submitted` — backpressure indicator.
- `redis.memory.usage{shard}` — capacity planning.
- `cassandra.write.latency` — durable store health.

**Tracing**

- One trace per score submission: validation → Kafka publish → aggregation → Redis ZADD → Cassandra write.

**Security**

- **Score endpoints are server-to-server only** — no client direct access.
- **JWT scope checks** — reading top-N is public; reading own rank requires auth; admin (modify scores) requires elevated role.
- **Audit log** — every score modification recorded with actor for cheating disputes.
- **PII isolation** — leaderboard stores only `user_id`; display names hydrated separately so a user can be renamed/deleted without reindexing leaderboards.
- **GDPR delete** — user deletion: ZREM from all boards; current_scores rows tombstoned.

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (100M users, 1M score updates/sec):**

- **Per-region Redis clusters** with cross-region async merge for global leaderboard.
- **Probabilistic data structures** for approximate ranks (HyperLogLog/CountMinSketch variants) when exact rank isn't needed.
- **Tiered storage** — only top 1M users live in Redis; users below rank 1M served from Cassandra with slightly higher latency.
- **Dedicated CDN tier** for top-N with edge compute serving JSON directly without origin hit.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **Daily/weekly window roll-over time** — UTC midnight isn't fair globally; per-region roll-over might be needed.
- **Tie-breaking** — timestamp-based wins favors early players; alternative is score-only with random ordering for ties.
- **Friend-group materialization threshold** — ~150 friends works on-the-fly; ~10K friends needs materialized view.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **Relational `ORDER BY score DESC`** — fine for top-100 read, O(N) for "my rank" — unacceptable for personalized queries.
- **In-memory app-tier rank computation** — doesn't scale across instances, loses on restart.
- **Single global ZSET for all leaderboards** — write hot-spot; partition by scope.
- **Trusting client-submitted scores** — cheating is rampant; server-validated only.
- **Real-time CDN purge on every score update** — 100K updates/sec would melt CDN; 10s TTL is the right trade-off.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Redis Sorted Sets** are the right primitive — O(log N) ZADD/ZRANK/ZREVRANGE.
- **One ZSET per (scope, time window)** — global, regional, daily, weekly, season; partitioning prevents single-key hot writes.
- **Tie-breaking via encoded score** — `score * 1e9 - timestamp_ms` so earlier-reach wins.
- **Kafka decouples submission from aggregation** — absorbs bursts, gives durable replay.
- **Cassandra is the durable backstop** — rebuild Redis on cold start from `current_scores`.
- **Top-N CDN-cached** with 10s TTL — absorbs ~95% of public-view traffic; per-user reads bypass.
- **Anti-cheat at submission boundary** — server-validated only; no client-submitted scores.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- Score semantics — monotonically increasing or arbitrary?
- Leaderboard scopes — global only or also regional, friends?
- Time windows — all-time, daily, weekly, seasonal?
- Tie-breaking rule?
- Anti-cheat — server-validated or client-trusted?

**Assumptions for this design**

10M total users, 1M DAU, 100K concurrent during tournaments. Score updates ~5K/sec average, 100K/sec at tournament peak. Boards: global all-time, daily, weekly, regional (10), friend-group on-the-fly. Tie-break by earlier-reach time. Sub-100ms p99 for write, sub-50ms for read.

**Quick capacity check**

- 700 MB Redis for the global ZSET; ~5 GB total across all boards
- 80K ZADD/sec per Redis instance, sharded cluster scales horizontally
- 100K writes/sec at peak handled by partitioning across boards
- Top-N read absorbed ~95% by CDN; origin sees a fraction

**The core decision — Redis Sorted Sets**

- Internally a skip list + hash table
- O(log N) for ZADD (update score), ZRANK (get rank), ZRANGE (get top-N or nearby slice)
- For 10M members that's ~23 operations per lookup vs 10 million for a SQL count
- Rejected SQL `ORDER BY score DESC` because "my rank" is O(N) (count of higher scores)
- Rejected in-memory app-tier rank because it doesn't survive restarts or scale across instances

**Partitioning by scope and time window**

- One ZSET per (board, time window): `lb:global:all-time`, `lb:global:daily:2026-04-21`, `lb:regional:us-west:all-time`
- Time-windowed boards roll over (daily at midnight UTC, weekly on Mondays); old keys retained with 30-day TTL
- BoardResolver computes which boards a score event affects — typically global + region + daily + weekly
- Friend-group is computed on the fly: ZMSCORE for each friend ID, sort in memory

**Tie-breaking via score encoding**

- `encoded_score = raw_score * 1e9 - (timestamp_ms - epoch)`
- For equal raw scores, earlier reach has higher encoded score
- Encoded value stays within 64-bit double precision

**High-level shape**

- Submit path: Game Service → Anti-Cheat validates → Kafka → Score Aggregator → ZADD across all relevant ZSETs + Cassandra write
- Read path top-N: CDN with 10s TTL → (on miss) Leaderboard API → ZREVRANGE on Redis
- Read path personalized: bypass CDN → Leaderboard API → ZREVRANK + ZRANGE for nearby slice
- Cassandra is the durable backstop; Redis can be rebuilt from `current_scores` on cold start

**LLD — clean abstractions**

- `LeaderboardStore` interface (RedisLeaderboardStore impl); in-memory TreeMap impl for tests
- `ScoreAggregator` is idempotent on event_id (ZADD same value is no-op; Cassandra upsert idempotent)
- `BoardResolver` extracts membership logic
- `ScoreEncoder` for tie-break encoding
- `CacheWarmer` rebuilds Redis from Cassandra on cold start

**Anti-cheat**

- Score endpoints are server-to-server only — no client direct access
- Game Service validates match outcome (replay or server simulation)
- Anti-Cheat module checks implausible growth, signatures, IP/device anomalies
- Suspicious scores quarantined for manual review before adding to leaderboard

**Failure handling**

- Redis down: reads serve from CDN; CacheWarmer rebuilds from Cassandra on recovery
- Kafka down: submission service buffers locally; returns 503 on overflow
- Cassandra down: Redis stays current; Cassandra writes accumulate in retry topic
- Aggregator crash: Kafka replay; ZADD and Cassandra upsert are idempotent
- Tournament burst: pre-scale, lower CDN TTL on tournament boards, more Kafka partitions

**Production extras**

- Top-N CDN with 10s TTL (1s during tournament finals)
- JWT scopes: public top-N; auth required for own-rank; elevated role for admin score modification
- Audit log of every score modification
- GDPR delete: ZREM from all boards on user deletion
- Display names stored separately so renames don't require reindexing

**At 10× scale**

- Per-region Redis clusters with cross-region async merge for global
- Tiered storage — only top 1M live in Redis, deeper served from Cassandra
- Edge compute on CDN serving top-N JSON without origin hit

**Recommendation**

**Redis Sorted Sets as the leaderboard primitive, partitioned per (scope, time window) ZSETs, Kafka decoupling submission from aggregation, Cassandra as the durable backstop with cold-start rebuild, CDN-cached top-N with 10s TTL, and server-validated anti-cheat at the submission boundary** — the same shape Steam, Epic, and Riot run for ranked play.

Each is its own ranked structure. Tie-breaking — two players score 9999. Rank is ambiguous unless we encode tiebreakers into the.

A leaderboard answers two distinct questions, both fast: "Top N players" — read-mostly, broadcast to millions of viewers. "What rank am I, and who's near me?" — personalized, computed per-user. The SQL approach (ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT N) handles the first acceptably until score updates flood in. The second — "my rank" — becomes O(N) (SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE score > my_score). At 10M users and 10K score updates/sec, this is the wrong shape. Why this isn't a solved problem just by "use Redis": Partitioning — there isn't one leaderboard. There's global, regional, country, friend-group, daily, weekly, all-time, season-X. Each is its own ranked structure. Tie-breaking — two players score 9999. Rank is ambiguous unless we encode tiebreakers into the.
Relational ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT N for rank-of-self (O(N) count of higher scores), or treating Redis as the source of truth with no durable backstop.

Redis Sorted Sets are the right primitive — O(log N) ZADD/ZRANK/ZREVRANGE. One ZSET per (scope, time window) — global, regional, daily, weekly, season; partitioning prevents single-key hot writes. Tie-breaking via encoded score — score * 1e9 - timestamp_ms so earlier-reach wins. Kafka decouples submission from aggregation — absorbs bursts, gives durable replay. Cassandra is the durable backstop — rebuild Redis on cold start from current_scores. Top-N CDN-cached with 10s TTL — absorbs ~95% of public-view traffic; per-user reads bypass. Anti-cheat at submission boundary — server-validated.

questions.question: Design a file storage service like Dropbox or Google Drive.
questions.title: Design a File Storage Service (Dropbox / Google Drive)
questions.direct_answer: Split files into **fixed-size chunks** (4 MB), upload them to **object storage** (S3) addressed by **content hash** (deduplication), and store metadata (file tree, versions, sharing) in a sharded **PostgreSQL** cluster. Use a **chunk-level diffing** algorithm so only changed chunks are transferred on update. Sync clients use a **long-poll/push channel** plus **per-user change journal** for incremental sync. Generate **pre-signed S3 URLs** for direct client upload/download to bypass the application tier. CDN-cache **read-only public-share** downloads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Chunk-based file representation, deduplication by content hash, metadata vs blob storage separation, sync protocol for clients, and pre-signed URL pattern.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Storing files as blobs in PostgreSQL, or uploading whole-file on every change (no chunk diffing).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss content-addressed storage for cross-user dedup, the file change journal for incremental sync, end-to-end encryption trade-offs, and consistent-prefix sharing semantics.

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
A file storage service looks like "upload a file, download a file." The operational reality:

- **Files are big and many** — hundreds of millions of users, billions of files, petabytes of data.
- **Sync is the user expectation** — not just upload/download, but "my change appears on all my devices in seconds."
- **Most data is already-stored data** — cross-user duplication is rampant (the same MP3, the same PDF, the same OS update). Naive storage costs you 5–10× more than necessary.
- **Updates are partial** — a 2 GB video edited at one frame shouldn't re-upload 2 GB.
- **Sharing has security and consistency requirements** — share a folder; two collaborators edit; the system must converge.
- **Direct client ↔ storage path** is mandatory — routing 100 GB through your application tier melts it.
- **Versioning** — "undo last week's deletion" is a feature; storage cost compounds.
- **Mobile clients** with intermittent connectivity, low bandwidth, and storage constraints.

The central architectural decisions: **separate metadata (small, structured, ACID) from blobs (huge, immutable, eventually consistent)**, **chunk files for dedup and diff-based sync**, **address chunks by content hash**, and **let clients talk directly to object storage via pre-signed URLs** rather than proxying through the app tier.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- **Folder hierarchy** — deep folders, paths up to N chars?
- **Sharing** — read-only public links, per-user permissions, group/team folders?
- **Versioning** — keep N versions, time-bounded retention?
- **Conflict resolution** — last-write-wins, or fork into "file (conflict copy).docx"?
- **Selective sync** — client picks subset of folders?
- **Trash/recycle bin** with restore?
- **End-to-end encryption** required?

**Non-functional**
- **Per-user storage quota**?
- **Per-file size limit** — typically GB-scale max?
- **Sync latency target** — sub-second for change notification, minutes for large transfers?
- **Bandwidth efficiency** — chunk diffing required?
- **Geographic distribution** — multi-region for latency?

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **500M total users**, **100M DAU**.
- **Average file size**: 1 MB; long tail to 10 GB per file; max 50 GB/file.
- **Per-user 100 GB free quota**, paid tiers up to 2 TB.
- **2 PB stored data growth per day**.
- **Chunk size: 4 MB fixed** — trade-off discussed below.
- **Content-addressed dedup** — chunks identified by SHA-256 of bytes; same chunk shared across users (with namespace isolation).
- **Sync latency**: change visible on second device within 2 seconds (small files), within minutes (large files).
- **Pre-signed S3 URLs** for direct client upload/download.
- **Versioning**: keep last 30 days of versions for paid users, 7 days for free.
- **Trash**: deleted files retained 30 days before purge.
- **Conflict resolution**: fork to "file (conflict copy from device X).ext" — never silently overwrite.
- **No E2EE in this v1** — server can read for thumbnailing, search, virus scan.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- Upload: 100M DAU × average 50 MB/day = 5 PB/day → ~580 GB/sec sustained ingestion. With dedup, perhaps 30% net new data → ~175 GB/sec to S3.
- Metadata writes: ~500K/sec (file creates, renames, moves, version bumps).
- Sync change events: ~1M/sec at peak (each change fans out to user's other devices).

**Storage**

- 500M users × average 50 GB used = **25 EB raw** before dedup.
- With chunk dedup (assume 30% reduction): **~17 EB net**.
- Metadata: 500M users × average 1000 files each = 500B files × ~500 bytes/row = **~250 TB metadata** in sharded PostgreSQL.

**Bandwidth**

- Direct client ↔ S3 transfer is ~580 GB/sec average — doesn't touch our app tier.
- App tier handles only metadata and small control-plane traffic — manageable.

**Sync fan-out**

- Average user has 3 devices. Each change → 2 push notifications.
- 1M changes/sec → ~2M push notifications/sec.

**Conclusion**: bytes scale via S3 (basically infinite); the engineering hardness is in metadata sharding, sync protocol latency, and chunk diffing efficiency.

sections.title: Why Chunking, Why 4 MB
sections.content:
**Why chunk** at all rather than storing whole files:

- **Deduplication** — if a 1 GB OS install package is uploaded by 1M users, we store 250 unique chunks (~1 GB total) instead of 1 PB.
- **Diff-based sync** — if a user edits a single page in a 1 GB PDF, only the affected chunks change; others stay deduplicated.
- **Resumable upload** — a flaky connection drops at chunk 47/256; resume from chunk 48.
- **Parallel transfer** — upload 32 chunks concurrently to saturate user bandwidth.

**Why 4 MB**:

- **Smaller** (e.g., 64 KB): too many chunks per file → huge metadata overhead, many round trips.
- **Larger** (e.g., 64 MB): less effective for partial edits; hurts dedup recall (hash collision space sparser).
- **4 MB** is industry sweet spot (Dropbox uses ~4 MB, S3's multipart minimum is 5 MB). Balances metadata cost against I/O efficiency.

**Variable-size content-defined chunking** (Rabin fingerprint) is a more sophisticated alternative — chunk boundaries chosen by content patterns rather than fixed offsets. Better dedup for files where insertions shift content (text edits). Adds complexity; we'd defer to v2.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
**Upload (initiation):**

```http
POST /api/v1/files
{
  "path": "/Documents/report.pdf",
  "size": 12345678,
  "chunk_hashes": [
    "sha256:abc123...",
    "sha256:def456...",
    ...
  ]
}

200 OK
{
  "file_id": "f_7Z3kY8",
  "upload_session": "sess_abc",
  "missing_chunks": [
    {
      "hash": "sha256:def456...",
      "upload_url": "https://s3.../chunks/df/def456?X-Amz-Signature=...&Expires=..."
    }
  ],
  "existing_chunks": ["sha256:abc123..."]
}
```

The server returns **only chunks not already present** — dedup happens at upload initiation. Client uploads missing chunks directly to S3 via pre-signed URLs.

**Upload completion:**

```http
POST /api/v1/files/{file_id}/commit
{
  "upload_session": "sess_abc"
}

201 Created
{
  "file_id": "f_7Z3kY8",
  "version": 1,
  "sha256": "sha256:full-file-hash"
}
```

**Download:**

```http
GET /api/v1/files/{file_id}

200 OK
{
  "file_id": "f_7Z3kY8",
  "path": "/Documents/report.pdf",
  "size": 12345678,
  "chunks": [
    {"hash": "sha256:abc123...", "url": "https://s3.../...?signature"},
    ...
  ]
}
```

Client downloads chunks directly from S3, in parallel.

**Sync (long-poll for changes since cursor):**

```http
GET /api/v1/sync/changes?cursor={opaque}&timeout=30s

200 OK
{
  "changes": [
    {"type":"created", "file_id":"...", "path":"..."},
    {"type":"updated", "file_id":"...", "version":2},
    {"type":"deleted", "file_id":"..."}
  ],
  "next_cursor": "opaque-token"
}
```

**Sharing:**

```http
POST /api/v1/files/{file_id}/share
{"with":"user_42","permission":"editor"}

POST /api/v1/files/{file_id}/public-link
{"expires_at":"2026-12-31"}
```

sections.title: Data Model
sections.content:
**Files** (PostgreSQL, sharded by `owner_id`):

```sql
CREATE TABLE files (
    file_id        VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
    parent_id      VARCHAR(64),                       -- folder hierarchy
    name           TEXT NOT NULL,
    is_folder      BOOLEAN DEFAULT false,
    current_version INT DEFAULT 1,
    size_bytes     BIGINT,
    full_hash      CHAR(64),                          -- sha256 of full file
    deleted_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,                       -- trash; null = live
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    updated_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX ON files (owner_id, parent_id, deleted_at);
```

**File versions** (tracks chunk lists per version):

```sql
CREATE TABLE file_versions (
    file_id        VARCHAR(64),
    version        INT,
    chunk_hashes   TEXT[],                            -- ordered list of chunk hashes
    size_bytes     BIGINT,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    created_by     BIGINT,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version)
);
```

**Chunks** (content-addressed; the dedup table):

```sql
CREATE TABLE chunks (
    chunk_hash     CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,              -- sha256
    s3_key         TEXT NOT NULL,                     -- e.g., "chunks/ab/abc123..."
    size_bytes     INT NOT NULL,
    ref_count      BIGINT DEFAULT 0,                  -- decremented on file deletion
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
```

**Sync change journal** (per-user log of changes for incremental sync):

```sql
CREATE TABLE sync_events (
    user_id        BIGINT,
    seq            BIGSERIAL,                         -- monotonic per user
    file_id        VARCHAR(64),
    event_type     VARCHAR(16),                       -- created, updated, deleted, moved
    occurred_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, seq)
);
```

**Shares**:

```sql
CREATE TABLE shares (
    file_id        VARCHAR(64),
    user_id        BIGINT,
    permission     VARCHAR(16),                       -- viewer, editor, owner
    granted_by     BIGINT,
    granted_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, user_id)
);

CREATE TABLE public_links (
    link_token     VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,
    file_id        VARCHAR(64),
    expires_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    permission     VARCHAR(16)
);
```

Relationships:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ FILES : owns
    USERS ||--o{ SHARES : participates
    USERS ||--o{ SYNC_EVENTS : journaled_for
    FILES ||--|{ FILE_VERSIONS : versioned_as
    FILES ||--o{ SHARES : shared
    FILE_VERSIONS }o--o{ CHUNKS : composed_of
    FILES ||--o{ PUBLIC_LINKS : exposed_via
    FILES {
        string file_id PK
        bigint owner_id FK
        string parent_id FK
        text name
        int current_version
    }
    FILE_VERSIONS {
        string file_id FK
        int version PK
        string_array chunk_hashes
        bigint size_bytes
    }
    CHUNKS {
        char64 chunk_hash PK
        text s3_key
        int size_bytes
        bigint ref_count
    }
    SYNC_EVENTS {
        bigint user_id FK
        bigserial seq PK
        string file_id FK
        string event_type
    }
```

sections.title: Chunk Dedup, Pre-Signed URLs, and Direct Transfer
sections.content:
**Content-addressed storage**:

- Chunk's S3 key = `chunks/{hash[:2]}/{hash}` (the prefix split keeps S3 partitions hot-spread).
- Same content always hashes to same key → same S3 object.
- A chunk is uploaded once across all users; subsequent users only update metadata refs.

**Dedup at the upload boundary**:

- Client computes SHA-256 of each 4 MB chunk before talking to server.
- Sends just the **hash list**.
- Server queries `chunks` table for existing hashes → returns pre-signed PUT URLs only for missing ones.
- Typical efficiency: ~30% of chunks already exist on a fresh-user upload of common files (OS installers, popular media); much higher for users syncing their own existing collection across devices.

**Cross-user dedup security**:

- A malicious user could probe for chunks they don't own ("do you have this hash?").
- Mitigation: chunks are namespaced under content hash but **access requires file metadata reference** — the user must own a file_version that references the chunk to be able to download it.
- The dedup test on upload doesn't reveal which user owns the duplicate.

**Pre-signed URLs**:

- Server uses S3 SDK to generate temporary signed URLs (15-minute expiry) bound to specific S3 key + HTTP method.
- Client uploads/downloads directly; bytes never traverse our app tier.
- Enables 100s of GB/sec aggregate throughput without scaling app servers for bandwidth.

**Reference counting and garbage collection**:

- Each `chunks.ref_count` decremented when a file version is hard-deleted.
- Background GC job removes chunks with `ref_count = 0` and `created_at < NOW() - 7 days`.
- 7-day grace prevents race with in-flight uploads.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design
Sync Protocol and Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
**Per-user change journal** (`sync_events`):

- Append-only log of changes affecting this user (their files, plus shared files they have access to).
- Each event has a monotonic sequence number per user.
- Client maintains a cursor (last-seen seq); polls or long-polls for new events.

**Long-poll over WebSocket-like push**:

- Client opens `GET /sync/changes?cursor=N&timeout=30s`.
- Server immediately returns events past cursor N if any exist.
- Otherwise holds the connection (registered in waiter map) up to 30s.
- On new event, server signals waiter and returns immediately.
- After 30s, returns empty batch; client reconnects.

**Why long-poll, not WebSocket:**

- Mobile clients connect/disconnect frequently; long-poll is simpler over flaky networks.
- Stateless server (any instance can serve any cursor request).
- HTTP keep-alive + idle-timeout is cheap.

**Conflict resolution:**

- Two devices edit the same file offline; both upload.
- Server compares **file_versions sequentially** — second commit detects parent version mismatch.
- Server creates a fork: `file (conflict copy from device X).docx` with the second upload's content.
- Both versions visible; user manually merges.
- This is the Dropbox model; Google Drive uses operational transformation for collaborative documents.

**Initial sync after fresh install**:

- Client starts with cursor 0.
- Server streams the user's full file tree as a sequence of `created` events in chunks (paginated).
- Client applies events to build local state.
- After initial catchup, normal long-poll loop.

sections.title: Storage Choice and Sharding
sections.content:
**Object storage (S3) for chunks**

- Effectively infinite capacity.
- 11 nines durability with cross-region replication.
- Direct client transfer via pre-signed URLs.
- Lifecycle policies move cold data to S3 Glacier for cost savings.

**PostgreSQL for metadata** — sharded by `owner_id`:

- ACID required for file tree mutations (rename, move, delete).
- Joins for shares, versions, etc.
- Sharding by owner keeps a user's entire tree on one shard — efficient for tree-walks.
- ~250 TB total metadata; ~256 shards at ~1 TB each.

**Cross-shard pain points**:

- Sharing across users hits two shards (file's owner shard for permission check, recipient's shard for journal entry). Use distributed transaction or eventually consistent share-grant.
- Shared folders: the folder lives on owner's shard; collaborators see it via a view-resolver that crosses shards on `getFile`. Adds latency for shared content.

**Redis for upload session state** (TTL 1 hour) and chunk-existence cache (avoids hammering PostgreSQL on the dedup check).

**Why not put metadata in DynamoDB?** Could work — KV access pattern is dominant. But the file tree (parent_id pointers, list children of folder) is a relational access pattern and benefits from PostgreSQL's JOINs and indexes.

**Why not store files in PostgreSQL** (BYTEA columns)? Doesn't scale past low-hundred-MB files; backups become impossible; replication lags grow; DB throughput becomes a bandwidth bottleneck.

sections.title: Caching, CDN, and Public Sharing
sections.content:
**App tier caches**:

- File metadata: Redis cache for hot files (5-minute TTL).
- Chunk-existence dedup cache: Redis bloom filter per shard — fast "definitely not present" check before hitting PostgreSQL.
- Share permission cache: Redis with explicit invalidation on permission change.

**CDN for public-share downloads**:

- Public shareable links (`/p/{link_token}`) resolve to the underlying file's chunks.
- For small public files (< 100 MB), CDN-cache the full file response.
- For large files, CDN caches chunk-by-chunk with long TTL (chunks are content-addressed and immutable).
- Massive offload for viral files (a popular shared photo can be served from CDN edge globally without origin hit).

**Hot file problem**:

- Viral public link sees millions of downloads.
- CDN absorbs the bulk; S3 bandwidth still rises.
- For extremely viral files, mirror chunks to additional S3 buckets and round-robin pre-signed URLs.

**Cold storage tiering**:

- Files unaccessed for > 90 days transitioned to S3 Standard-IA (cheaper, slightly higher latency).
- Versions older than 30 days moved to Glacier (much cheaper, retrieval ~hours).
- Saves significant cost at petabyte scale.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**S3 unavailable**

- New uploads fail; client retries with exponential backoff.
- Downloads fall back to cross-region replica bucket.
- Metadata service stays up; file tree browsing still works.

**Metadata DB shard failure**

- Affected slice of users sees `503` on metadata operations.
- Read replicas serve stale browse for the failure window.
- Multi-AZ failover (~30s); user retries succeed after.

**Sync service crash**

- Long-poll connections drop; clients reconnect and resume from cursor.
- No data loss; in-flight events are committed to `sync_events` before the connection returns.

**Upload session expiration**

- Sessions expire after 1 hour.
- Client retries from scratch (idempotent on chunk hashes — chunks already uploaded are still in S3).

**Partial upload**

- Client uploaded 8 of 10 chunks then crashed.
- Chunks have `ref_count = 0` for 7-day grace before GC.
- Client retries within session window: re-checks dedup, only missing chunks remain to upload.

**Conflict during commit**

- Two devices commit the same file_id with different parent versions.
- Optimistic version check: second commit gets `409 Conflict`.
- Client receives conflict; creates a fork copy locally and uploads it as a new file.

**GC race**

- A chunk being uploaded by user A is referenced by user B's just-committed file just as GC runs.
- 7-day grace + ref_count check at GC time prevents premature deletion.
- Defense-in-depth: GC takes a brief lock on the chunk row before delete.

**Mobile offline**

- Client queues local changes; on reconnect, replays uploads with same chunk hashes.
- Sync cursor advances after successful catchup.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `upload.dedup.hit_rate` — % of chunks already present; bandwidth savings.
- `sync.poll.latency` p99 — SLO < 2s for change visibility.
- `s3.upload.success_rate` and `s3.download.success_rate`.
- `metadata.db.shard.qps` and `metadata.db.shard.replication_lag`.
- `chunk.gc.deleted_per_day` — storage reclamation health.
- `share.permission.cache.miss_rate`.

**Tracing**

- Trace from client → metadata service → (parallel) S3 ops; correlation ID flows through pre-signed URL custom headers.

**Security**

- **OAuth/OIDC** for client authentication; fine-grained per-file permissions enforced server-side on every metadata op.
- **Pre-signed URLs are short-lived** (15 min) and bound to specific S3 key.
- **Permission checks at metadata layer**, not in S3 — S3 sees only requests with valid signed URLs; the URL signing process verifies permission.
- **Encryption at rest** — S3 server-side encryption (KMS); per-customer keys for enterprise tier.
- **Encryption in transit** — TLS for all client ↔ S3 traffic.
- **Virus scan** at upload — chunk content scanned async; flagged files quarantined.
- **DLP / PII detection** for compliance use cases.
- **Audit log** of every share/permission change for enterprise compliance.
- **End-to-end encryption** (zero-knowledge) is a tier upgrade — client encrypts before upload; server can't index, scan, or thumbnail. Major product trade-off.

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (5B users, 50 PB/day):**

- **Geo-distributed metadata** with CRDT-based eventual consistency for shared folders.
- **Multi-region S3** with intelligent client routing — always upload to the nearest region; replicate async.
- **Variable-size content-defined chunking** (Rabin fingerprinting) for better dedup on edited text/code files.
- **Tiered chunk caches** at edge POPs for frequently-downloaded files.
- **WebSocket sync** for low-latency change push to active sessions; long-poll only as fallback.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **4 MB chunk size** — smaller chunks (1 MB) for sync-heavy workloads (frequent partial edits); larger (16 MB) for media archives.
- **Optimistic vs pessimistic conflict resolution** — forking on conflict works for documents; collaborative editing wants OT or CRDT.
- **Permission check granularity** — per-folder inheritance vs per-file is a UX vs operational complexity trade-off.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **Storing files in PostgreSQL** — doesn't scale; bandwidth bottleneck.
- **Routing bytes through application servers** — melts the app tier.
- **No chunking** (whole-file uploads) — no resumability, no diff-sync, dedup only at file-hash level (much less effective).
- **No content-addressed dedup** — storage cost doubles or triples; cross-user duplicates rampant.
- **Synchronous virus scan blocking upload** — latency unacceptable; scan async and quarantine if flagged.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **4 MB fixed chunks, content-addressed by SHA-256** — enables cross-user dedup, diff-based sync, and resumable uploads.
- **Pre-signed S3 URLs** for direct client ↔ storage transfer — bytes never traverse our app tier.
- **Sharded PostgreSQL for metadata** (file tree, versions, shares, sync journal); S3 for blobs.
- **Per-user change journal** with monotonic sequence + long-poll for sync — simple, mobile-friendly, stateless server.
- **Conflict resolution by forking** to a `(conflict copy)` file — never silently overwrite.
- **Reference-counted chunks with 7-day grace GC** — safe deletion without race conditions.
- **CDN cache for public-share downloads**; chunks are immutable so caching is trivial.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- Folder hierarchy depth, sharing model (read-only links, per-user, group folders)?
- Versioning — keep how many versions, time-bounded?
- Conflict resolution — last-write-wins or fork to conflict copy?
- Selective sync, trash, public links?
- End-to-end encryption?

**Assumptions for this design**

500M users, 100M DAU, average file 1 MB with long tail to GBs, 100 GB free quota, 4 MB fixed chunks. 2 PB/day growth. Sub-2-second sync visibility for small files. Pre-signed S3 URLs for direct transfer. Conflict forking. No E2EE in v1.

**Quick capacity check**

- 5 PB/day uploads, ~30% net new after dedup = ~175 GB/sec to S3
- 25 EB raw before dedup, ~17 EB after
- Metadata: 500B files, ~250 TB across sharded PostgreSQL (256 shards at ~1 TB each)
- Sync fan-out: ~2M push notifications/sec
- Critical: bytes go directly client ↔ S3, never through our app tier

**The central decisions**

1. Chunk files into 4 MB pieces — enables cross-user dedup, diff-sync, resumable uploads, parallel transfer
2. Address chunks by SHA-256 of bytes — same content always hashes to same key, so dedup is automatic
3. Separate metadata (sharded PostgreSQL) from blobs (S3)
4. Pre-signed S3 URLs for direct client transfer — bytes never traverse app servers

**Why 4 MB chunks**

- Smaller (64KB): too many chunks per file, huge metadata overhead
- Larger (64MB): hurts partial-edit dedup
- 4 MB is the industry sweet spot (Dropbox uses ~4 MB)
- Variable-size content-defined chunking (Rabin) is better for edited text but more complex; defer to v2

**Upload flow — step by step**

1. Client computes SHA-256 of each 4 MB chunk locally
2. Client POSTs the hash list to Upload Service
3. Server checks `chunks` table; returns pre-signed PUT URLs only for missing chunks
4. Client uploads missing chunks directly to S3 in parallel
5. Client commits; server creates new file_version row, increments chunk ref counts, publishes change event

**Download flow**

- Server returns ordered chunk list with pre-signed GET URLs
- Client downloads chunks in parallel from S3
- App tier handles only metadata; bandwidth scales via S3

**Sync flow — long-poll with per-user journal**

- File change → Kafka → SyncService writes to `sync_events` for affected users (owner + collaborators)
- Client maintains a cursor (last-seen seq); calls `GET /sync/changes?cursor=N&timeout=30s`
- Server returns immediately if events exist; otherwise holds connection up to 30s, signals on new event
- Long-poll over WebSocket because mobile clients reconnect frequently and stateless server is simpler
- Push notification fires for offline devices

**Conflict resolution**

- Two devices edit the same file offline; both upload
- Optimistic version check: second commit detects parent version mismatch, creates a fork as `(conflict copy from device X).docx`
- User manually merges — same as Dropbox model
- Google Docs-style operational transformation is a separate beast; out of scope here

**Data model**

- `files` (sharded by owner_id) — file tree, current_version pointer
- `file_versions` — ordered chunk_hashes per version
- `chunks` — the dedup table; chunk_hash PK, s3_key, ref_count
- `sync_events` — per-user append-only journal
- `shares` and `public_links` — access control

**LLD — clean abstractions**

- `ChunkRegistry` interface — PostgreSQL impl, could swap to DynamoDB for higher hash-lookup scale
- `PresignedUrlFactory` interface — S3 impl, could swap to GCS or Azure
- `UploadSession` server-side state tracks claimed chunks
- `SyncService` with a waiter registry for long-poll efficiency
- Garbage collector with 7-day grace runs separately

**Storage choice rationale**

- S3 for chunks: infinite capacity, 11-nines durability, lifecycle policies for cold tier
- PostgreSQL for metadata: ACID for tree mutations, JOINs for shares/versions, sharded by owner_id
- Redis for upload sessions, dedup bloom filter, share permission cache
- Rejected files-in-PostgreSQL — doesn't scale past low-hundred-MB; backups impossible

**Reference-counted chunks**

- Each commit increments ref_count for chunks; each delete decrements
- Chunks with ref_count = 0 for > 7 days are GC'd
- 7-day grace prevents race with in-flight uploads

**Failure handling**

- S3 down: cross-region failover; metadata still works
- DB shard down: read replicas serve stale browse; multi-AZ failover ~30s
- Upload session expires: client retries from scratch (chunks already uploaded skip dedup)
- Conflict at commit: 409 Conflict; client forks locally
- Mobile offline: client queues changes, replays on reconnect

**Production extras**

- TLS everywhere; OAuth/OIDC for clients
- Pre-signed URLs short-lived (15 min) and bound to specific S3 key
- S3 server-side encryption (KMS); per-customer keys for enterprise
- Async virus scan with quarantine on flag
- Audit log for enterprise compliance
- Lifecycle policies move cold files to Standard-IA / Glacier

**At 10× scale**

- Geo-distributed metadata with CRDTs for shared folders
- Multi-region S3 with nearest-region client routing
- Variable-size content-defined chunking for better text/code dedup
- Edge POP chunk caches for popular downloads
- WebSocket sync for active sessions

**Recommendation**

**4 MB content-addressed chunks deduped at the upload boundary, sharded PostgreSQL metadata + S3 blobs with pre-signed URLs for direct client transfer, per-user long-poll sync journal, reference-counted chunks with grace-period GC, and CDN-cached public shares** — the same shape Dropbox, OneDrive, and Box run in production.

questions.title: Design a Video Streaming Platform (YouTube / Netflix)
questions.direct_answer: Ingest uploaded videos into an **async transcoding pipeline** that produces multiple bitrate ladders (240p–4K) in **HLS/DASH** segment format. sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
Video looks like "upload, transcode, serve." The hard parts:

- **Bandwidth is the dominant cost** — a major streaming platform spends more on egress than on compute. Architecture is shaped by where bytes flow.
- **One source video, many output renditions** — 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K, multiple codecs (H.264, H.265, AV1), audio variants. A single 10-min upload becomes 50+ output files.
- **Adaptive bitrate (ABR)** — the player switches bitrate per 2-10 second segment based on measured bandwidth. Requires segmented file format (HLS/DASH) with manifest files.
- **CDN is non-negotiable** — originating video from a single region to a global audience is impossible. Multi-tier caching (edge → regional → origin) is mandatory.
- **Long-tail viewing distribution** — a few videos go viral; most are watched rarely. Storage tiering and caching strategy must reflect this.
- **Live streaming is a different beast** — sub-5-second latency for chat-relevant streams (Twitch); minute-scale for traditional broadcast.
- **Content protection** — DRM (Widevine, PlayReady, FairPlay) for premium content; signed URLs for free content.
- **Recommendations and search** — related to the platform, but a separate ML system; we touch the integration boundary.

The central architectural decisions: **how the transcoding pipeline scales** (chunked parallel transcoding), **how to deliver bytes** (CDN topology + ABR), **how to handle live separately from VOD**, and **how to keep metadata and analytics decoupled from the bandwidth-heavy serving path**.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- **VOD only, live, or both**? They differ significantly in pipeline shape.
- **Resolutions and codecs** — 4K HDR? AV1 in addition to H.264?
- **DRM** required for premium content?
- **Captions / subtitles** — burned-in, sidecar files, multiple languages?
- **User-generated content** (YouTube model) or curated catalog (Netflix)?
- **Comments, likes, recommendations** — in scope or separate?
- **Offline downloads** for mobile (Netflix-style)?

**Non-functional**
- **DAU and concurrent viewers** — drives CDN sizing.
- **Hours uploaded per minute** (YouTube reportedly hundreds) — drives transcoding capacity.
- **Per-stream latency** — broadcast-grade live (~30 s) vs ultra-low-latency live (~3 s)?
- **Geographic distribution** — global from day 1?
- **Storage retention** — keep all uploads forever or expire after N years?
- **Per-viewer bandwidth budget** — 5 Mbps for 1080p is typical.

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **VOD primary, with optional live channel**.
- **YouTube-style UGC** with moderation and recommendations.
- **Resolutions**: 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 1440p, 4K. Codecs: H.264 (universal), H.265 (mobile efficiency), AV1 (modern browsers; saves ~30% bandwidth).
- **HLS** as the primary streaming protocol (works on Safari natively); DASH alongside.
- **DRM optional** — supported but not required for v1 (assume mostly free UGC).
- **500M DAU**, **100M concurrent viewers** at peak.
- **500 hours uploaded per minute** (matches YouTube's reported scale).
- **4-6 second segment duration** for HLS/DASH (ABR responsiveness vs overhead trade-off).
- **Sub-2 second start-up latency** (time to first frame after click).
- **Multi-CDN** for resilience and cost optimization.
- **Storage tiering** — hot in S3 Standard, warm in S3 Standard-IA, cold (rarely watched) in Glacier.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- Uploads: 500 hours/min ÷ 60 = ~8.3 hours of new content per second → at average 100 MB/min source = ~14 GB/sec ingest.
- Transcoded outputs (~10 renditions): ~50 GB/sec produced for storage.
- Concurrent viewers: 100M peak. Average bitrate 2 Mbps (mix of resolutions) → **200 Tbps egress** at peak — essentially all served from CDN edge.

**Storage**

- New video per day: 500 hr/min × 1440 min = 720,000 hours/day × 1 GB per hour (compressed across all renditions, mid-resolution average) → **~720 TB/day net new**.
- 5-year horizon: ~1.3 EB. Stored in S3 with lifecycle policies; hot subset on edge cache.

**Transcoding compute**

- 8.3 hours of video per second of wall-clock ingest.
- Each output rendition takes roughly 1× source duration on a single CPU (for fast preset); chunked parallel processing distributes this.
- Need ~50,000 transcoding cores during peak; auto-scaled.

**CDN**

- 200 Tbps egress — served from ~1000+ edge POPs globally with multi-tier caching.
- Hit rate at edge: ~80% for top videos; tail served from regional + origin.
- Origin egress: ~40 Tbps (20% of total) — still huge; multi-region origin distribution.

**Conclusion**: bandwidth dominates. Decisions are made first about CDN topology and segment storage; transcoding is large-scale-batch; metadata is comparatively small.

sections.title: Why HLS/DASH and Adaptive Bitrate
sections.content:
**The old way**: a single MP4 file streamed via progressive download. Problems: no bitrate adaptation (a 1080p file is unwatchable on a slow connection), no fast seek, no DRM-friendly format, no live support.

**HLS (Apple) and DASH (open standard)** solve this with the same model:

- **Source video chopped into 4-6 second segments** (`.ts` for HLS, `.m4s` for DASH).
- **Multiple bitrate ladders** — 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, etc. Each rendition has its own segment files.
- **Manifest file** (`.m3u8` for HLS, `.mpd` for DASH) lists all renditions and their segments.

**Adaptive Bitrate (ABR)** — the client player:

1. Fetches the manifest.
2. Picks an initial rendition (often start low for fast startup).
3. After each segment, measures: download bandwidth, buffer level, current bitrate.
4. **Scales up** if buffer is healthy and bandwidth supports a higher rendition.
5. **Scales down** if buffer drops or bandwidth degrades.
6. Switches happen between segments — no re-buffer required.

**Why segment length matters**:

- **Shorter** (2 s): faster ABR response, lower latency for live, more manifest overhead.
- **Longer** (10 s): better compression efficiency, lower per-segment overhead, slower ABR response.
- **4-6 s** is the VOD sweet spot. Live streams often use 2 s with low-latency HLS extensions.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
**Upload (init):**

```http
POST /api/v1/videos
{
  "title": "...",
  "description": "...",
  "visibility": "public",
  "size_bytes": 1234567890
}

201 Created
{
  "video_id": "vid_7Z3kY8",
  "upload_url": "https://upload.../?signature",
  "status": "awaiting_upload"
}
```

Client PUTs the source file to the pre-signed URL.

**Status query:**

```http
GET /api/v1/videos/{video_id}

200 OK
{
  "video_id": "vid_7Z3kY8",
  "status": "transcoded",   // uploading | scanning | transcoding | transcoded | failed
  "available_renditions": ["240p","360p","480p","720p","1080p"],
  "manifest_url": "https://cdn.../vid_7Z3kY8/master.m3u8",
  "thumbnails": [...]
}
```

**Watch (manifest fetch):**

```http
GET https://cdn.example.com/vid_7Z3kY8/master.m3u8

200 OK  Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:6
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=426x240
240p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1500000,RESOLUTION=854x480
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3000000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=6000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8
```

The player picks one variant; fetches its segment manifest:

```http
GET https://cdn.example.com/vid_7Z3kY8/720p/index.m3u8

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6
#EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE:0
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg-000.ts
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg-001.ts
...
```

Then fetches `.ts` segments in order; switches between renditions on bandwidth changes.

**Live channel:**

```http
GET /live/{channel_id}/master.m3u8     (rolling manifest; segments expire)
```

sections.content:
**Video metadata** in PostgreSQL (sharded by `video_id` hash):

```sql
CREATE TABLE videos (
    video_id          VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,
    uploader_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
    title             TEXT,
    description       TEXT,
    visibility        VARCHAR(16),       -- public | unlisted | private
    duration_sec      INT,

    published_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,

CREATE TABLE video_renditions (
    video_id          VARCHAR(64),
    rendition         VARCHAR(16),       -- 240p, 360p, ...

    bitrate_bps       BIGINT,
    s3_prefix         TEXT,              -- chunks live under this prefix

sections.title: Transcoding Pipeline — Chunked Parallel Processing
sections.content:
A 4-hour movie at single-stream FFmpeg = 4 hours wall clock per rendition. With 10 renditions, that's 40 hours per upload — unacceptable for a uploader expecting same-day availability.

**Chunked transcoding**:

1. **Split the source** into 30-second chunks based on keyframes (independent decode units).
2. **Distribute chunks to a worker pool** (containerized FFmpeg jobs).
3. **Each worker transcodes its chunk** to all required renditions.
4. **Stitch outputs** back into segmented HLS/DASH files.
5. **Generate manifests** referencing the segment files.

A 4-hour movie with 480 chunks running on 480 workers completes in ~30 seconds wall clock per rendition.

**Job scheduling**:

- Kafka topic `transcode.tasks` partitioned by `video_id` (keeps a video's chunks co-located for stitching).
- Workers consume via consumer groups; auto-scale based on queue depth.
- Each task carries: source S3 key, time range (start/end seconds), output S3 prefix, target rendition spec.
- On worker crash, Kafka redelivery guarantees retry.

**Quality validation**:

- Compute **VMAF (Video Multimethod Assessment Fusion)** scores comparing source vs each rendition.
- Reject renditions below quality threshold (e.g., VMAF < 70).
- Flagged videos can be re-encoded with higher bitrates.

**Adaptive ladder per video**:

- Static ladder (240p → 4K) is suboptimal — a screencast doesn't need 4K, but a 4K HDR film does.
- **Per-title encoding** (Netflix's approach): analyze content complexity per video and choose bitrate per rendition that achieves target VMAF — saves significant bandwidth on simple content.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design of the Transcode Pipeline
CDN Strategy and Multi-Tier Caching
sections.content:
**Multi-tier CDN topology:**

- **Edge POPs** (1000+ globally): cache top videos and recently accessed content. ~80% hit rate for hot videos.
- **Regional mid-tier** (~50 sites): backstop for edge misses; aggregates traffic before hitting origin.
- **Origin** (cloud object store, multi-region replicated): final source of truth.

**Why multi-tier matters:**

- Without mid-tier, every edge miss hits origin; viral video could overwhelm origin egress.
- Mid-tier adds another caching layer, reducing origin egress to ~5–10% of total.

**Manifest vs segment caching:**

- **Master manifests** rarely change for VOD — cache for hours.
- **Variant manifests** also stable for VOD; live manifests roll constantly (cache for ~2x segment duration).
- **Segments are immutable** — cache forever; the URL itself is content-addressable (segment number + rendition).

**Multi-CDN steering:**

- Use 2–3 CDN providers (Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly).
- DNS-based or client-side steering picks fastest/cheapest CDN per viewer.
- Resilience: one CDN outage doesn't take down playback.
- Cost: arbitrage across providers based on regional pricing.

**Cache key design:**

- `vid_7Z3kY8/720p/seg-042.ts` is fully content-addressable; no headers/auth in cache key.
- Signed URLs expire on the request, but the underlying segment is the same bytes for everyone — CDN caches the segment, not the signed URL.

sections.title: Storage Choice and Tiering
sections.content:
**Object storage (S3) for source + segments**:

- Effectively infinite capacity.
- Cross-region replication for resilience.
- Lifecycle policies for tiering.

**Tiered storage**:

- **Hot** (S3 Standard): all segments for top 10% of videos by recency + popularity.
- **Warm** (S3 Standard-IA): segments for the long tail; slightly higher per-GB cost on retrieval but ~50% cheaper to store.
- **Cold** (Glacier Deep Archive): videos unwatched in 6+ months; minutes-to-hours retrieval, very cheap storage.
- **Source files**: kept in IA after transcoding completes (rare to re-transcode); deleted after 90 days for free-tier UGC.

**Per-rendition tiering**:

- Lowest renditions (240p, 360p) are hot — served to mobile users on slow connections, viewed disproportionately.
- Highest renditions (4K) for niche content can be in Warm.

**Why PostgreSQL (sharded) for metadata**:

- Strong consistency on video state transitions (transcoding → available).
- JOINs for catalog queries.
- Sharded by `video_id` hash; 256+ shards.

**Why Cassandra for view events**:

- Write-heavy (billions of events/day).
- Time-series access pattern (events for video X in time range Y).
- Wide-column store fits naturally; no JOINs needed.

sections.title: Live Streaming — The Different Beast
sections.content:
Live differs from VOD in critical ways:

- **Latency-sensitive** — viewer expectation: 10–30 s for traditional broadcast, 2–5 s for chat-relevant streams (Twitch).
- **Continuous ingest** — source is always-on, not a finite upload.
- **Manifest evolves** — new segments appear constantly; old ones expire.
- **Failure recovery** — must continue serving even if a transcoder crashes mid-stream.

**Live pipeline:**

- **Ingest server** (RTMP, SRT, or WebRTC) accepts the broadcaster's source stream.
- **Live transcoder** processes the incoming stream in real-time, producing renditions with ~2–6 s segments.
- **Origin server** publishes evolving HLS/DASH manifest with rolling segment list.
- **CDN** caches segments briefly (TTL = 2x segment duration); manifest TTL is short or `no-cache` with revalidation.

**Low-latency HLS / LL-HLS**:

- Adds **partial segments** (~200 ms each) so the player can start showing content before a full segment is ready.
- Server pushes partial segment updates via HTTP/2 Server Push or similar.
- Reduces glass-to-glass latency from ~30 s to ~3 s.

**WebRTC for sub-second**:

- For chat-relevant interactivity (~500 ms latency), WebRTC bypasses HLS entirely.
- Used for one-to-few or interactive broadcast (one-to-many WebRTC requires a Selective Forwarding Unit).
- Trade-off: more complex infrastructure; harder to scale to massive concurrency.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**Transcoding worker crash mid-chunk**

- Kafka redelivers chunk task to another worker.
- FFmpeg job is idempotent on output S3 key (overwrites are safe).
- Coordinator deduplicates completion events.

**Origin S3 outage**

- CDN serves cached content; ~80–95% of requests succeed from cache.
- New uploads fail; transcoding queues stall.
- Multi-region origin replication mitigates: failover to alternate region.

**CDN edge POP failure**

- DNS routes to next-nearest POP.
- Multi-CDN steering picks alternate provider for affected viewers.

**Player buffer underrun**

- ABR drops to lower rendition.
- If buffer empties, player shows spinner and pauses; resumes on next segment.
- Viewer-side metric (`rebuffer_ratio`) is the primary quality signal.

**Live stream disconnect from broadcaster**

- Ingest server sends end-of-stream marker; manifest finalizes.
- Viewers either see playback end or auto-reconnect for next live event.

**Viral video traffic spike**

- CDN absorbs nearly all of it (segments are immutable; cache works perfectly).
- Origin sees minor uptick; multi-region origin spreads the load.
- Per-title bitrate ladder may need re-encoding if content unexpectedly demands higher quality.

**Bad transcode (artifacts, sync issues)**

- VMAF check catches it; flagged for re-encode.
- Manual review for high-stakes content (premium catalog).
- Operator can roll back a rendition by removing it from the manifest until fixed.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `playback.startup_latency` p50/p99 — SLO < 2s.
- `playback.rebuffer_ratio` — target < 0.5%.
- `playback.bitrate_p50` — user-perceived quality.
- `cdn.hit_rate{layer=edge|regional}`.
- `transcoding.lag_seconds` — from upload-complete to all-renditions-available.
- `transcoding.vmaf_p50{rendition}`.
- `live.glass_to_glass_latency` (live only).
- `origin.egress_gbps` — cost driver.

**Tracing**

- Per-playback session trace: manifest fetch → segment fetches → ABR decisions → buffer state → errors. Crucial for diagnosing playback issues at the user level.

**Security**

- **Pre-signed CDN URLs** with 1-hour expiry for premium content.
- **DRM**: Widevine (Chrome/Android), PlayReady (Edge), FairPlay (Safari). Multi-DRM packaging during transcoding.
- **Token-based authorization** at CDN edge — verifies entitlement (geo, subscription, age-gate).
- **Geo-blocking** — license-required content blocked in unauthorized regions; enforced at CDN edge.
- **Hot-link prevention** — referrer/CORS check + signed URLs.
- **Content moderation** — ML-based scan of uploaded content; manual review for flagged.
- **Fingerprinting** — detect re-uploads of copyrighted content (Content ID at YouTube).

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (1B concurrent peak):**

- **Push more aggressive caching to ISP-embedded servers** (Netflix Open Connect appliances).
- **AV1 default codec** for ~30% bandwidth reduction on supported clients.
- **Per-viewer rendition switching prediction** using ML on past playback behavior.
- **Edge transcoding** for live (low-latency push to nearby POPs without origin round trip).

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **Static rendition ladder vs per-title encoding** — per-title saves bandwidth significantly but adds analysis cost.
- **HLS-only vs HLS + DASH + LL-HLS + WebRTC** — protocol matrix is operational complexity; pick what your client base actually needs.
- **Single CDN vs multi-CDN** — multi-CDN is resilience but doubles tooling.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **Single MP4 file streaming** — no bitrate adaptation; breaks on slow connections.
- **App-tier transcoding without chunking** — single-stream FFmpeg makes long videos unavailable for hours.
- **Routing video bytes through application servers** — melts the app tier; CDN exists for this exact reason.
- **Synchronous transcoding** before returning 201 to uploader — large videos take minutes; UX requires async with status polling.
- **Storing transcoded outputs in PostgreSQL** — wrong tool entirely.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HLS/DASH segmented format with adaptive bitrate** — player switches renditions per 4-6s segment based on bandwidth.
- **Async chunked transcoding pipeline** — source split by keyframes; workers process in parallel; outputs stitched into HLS/DASH manifests.
- **Per-title encoding** with VMAF validation — bitrate ladder tuned per video to optimize bandwidth vs quality.
- **Multi-tier CDN** (edge → regional → origin) with multi-CDN steering for resilience and cost.
- **Tiered object storage** (Hot/Warm/Cold S3 + Glacier) matches the long-tail viewing distribution.
- **Live is a separate pipeline** — RTMP/SRT ingest, real-time transcoding, rolling manifest, LL-HLS for low latency.
- **Metadata in sharded PostgreSQL; view events in Cassandra** — different access patterns, different stores.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- VOD only, live, or both?
- Resolutions and codecs — 4K HDR, AV1 alongside H.264?
- DRM required?
- UGC (YouTube) or curated catalog (Netflix)?
- Captions, recommendations, offline downloads in scope?
- Latency requirement for live?

**Assumptions for this design**

VOD primary with optional live. UGC like YouTube. Resolutions 240p–4K, codecs H.264 + H.265 + AV1. HLS primary with DASH alongside. 500M DAU, 100M concurrent peak. 500 hours uploaded per minute. Sub-2-second startup. Multi-CDN. Tiered storage.

**Quick capacity check**

- Egress: 100M concurrent × 2 Mbps avg = 200 Tbps at peak — essentially all from CDN edge
- Storage: 720 TB/day net new; ~1.3 EB over 5 years
- Transcoding: ~50,000 cores at peak with chunked parallelism
- Bandwidth dominates the cost — CDN topology and caching are the first decisions

**Why HLS/DASH and adaptive bitrate**

- Source video chopped into 4-6s segments; multiple bitrate ladders
- Manifest file lists all renditions and their segments
- Player measures bandwidth, switches renditions per segment
- Rejected single-MP4 streaming — no bitrate adaptation, unwatchable on slow connections, no DRM-friendly format

**Transcoding pipeline — chunked parallel**

- Single-stream FFmpeg on a 4-hour movie takes 4 hours per rendition; with 10 renditions that's 40 hours — unacceptable
- Split source by keyframes into 30-second chunks; distribute to worker pool; each worker transcodes its chunk to all renditions; stitch outputs back into HLS/DASH segments
- 480 workers process a 4-hour movie in ~30 seconds wall clock per rendition
- Per-title encoding (Netflix's approach): analyze content complexity, pick bitrate per rendition that hits target VMAF — saves bandwidth on simple content
- VMAF scores below threshold flag for re-encode

**High-level shape**

- Upload: pre-signed S3 URL → source upload → enqueue chunk tasks to Kafka → worker pool transcodes → outputs to S3 → packager generates manifests → metadata service marks available
- Playback: player fetches master manifest from CDN edge → picks rendition → fetches segment manifest + segments via CDN → origin only on edge miss
- Analytics: player emits view events to ingestion service → Cassandra → aggregator rolls up periodic stats to PostgreSQL

**CDN strategy — multi-tier and multi-CDN**

- Multi-tier: 1000+ edge POPs → ~50 regional mid-tiers → multi-region origin
- Edge hit rate ~80% for hot videos; mid-tier reduces origin egress further to ~5-10% of total
- Multi-CDN (2-3 providers) for resilience and cost arbitrage
- Segments are immutable and content-addressable; cache key is `videoId/rendition/segNum`; cache forever
- Manifests have shorter TTL (live: ~2x segment duration; VOD: hours)

**Storage tiering**

- Hot S3 Standard for top 10% by recency/popularity
- Warm S3 Standard-IA for the long tail (~50% cheaper)
- Cold Glacier for unwatched 6+ months
- Source files kept in IA after transcoding; deleted after 90 days for free-tier UGC

**Data model**

- `videos` (sharded PostgreSQL) — metadata, status, source key
- `video_renditions` — per-rendition info: codec, bitrate, S3 prefix
- `view_events` (Cassandra) — wide-column, partitioned by (video_id, time bucket)
- `video_stats` — aggregated counters for fast read

**LLD — clean abstractions**

- `StorageClient` interface (S3 impl; could swap to GCS)
- `FfmpegRunner` for transcoding; isolated for A/B-testing encoder versions or hardware
- `QualityValidator` for VMAF/PSNR/SSIM
- `TranscodingCoordinator` tracks chunk completion per video; finalizes when all chunks land
- `HlsPackager` builds manifests
- Per-title bitrate selection added in scheduler before publishing tasks

**Live streaming — different beast**

- Continuous ingest via RTMP/SRT/WebRTC; real-time transcoding; rolling manifest with segment expiry
- Glass-to-glass latency: ~30s for traditional, ~3s for low-latency HLS, ~500ms for WebRTC
- LL-HLS uses partial segments (~200ms each) pushed via HTTP/2 Server Push
- WebRTC for sub-second interactive (chat-relevant); needs SFU for one-to-many

**Failure handling**

- Transcoder crash: Kafka redelivers; FFmpeg output is idempotent on S3 key
- Origin outage: CDN serves cached content; multi-region origin failover
- CDN POP failure: DNS routes to next POP; multi-CDN picks alternate provider
- Player buffer underrun: ABR drops rendition; on empty, brief spinner
- Bad transcode: VMAF catches; flag for re-encode; remove from manifest until fixed
- Viral spike: CDN absorbs (immutable segments cache perfectly)

**Production extras**

- DRM (Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay) packaged at transcode time for premium content
- Token-based CDN edge authorization for entitlements (geo, subscription, age-gate)
- Multi-DRM, geo-blocking, hot-link prevention
- ML-based content moderation; manual review for flagged
- Content fingerprinting for copyright detection
- Per-playback distributed tracing for debugging quality issues

**At 10× scale**

- ISP-embedded servers (Netflix Open Connect)
- AV1 default for bandwidth savings
- ML-based per-viewer rendition prediction
- Edge transcoding for live

**Recommendation**

**Async chunked transcoding pipeline producing HLS/DASH segments with per-title bitrate ladders, multi-tier multi-CDN delivery, adaptive bitrate playback, tiered S3 storage matching the long-tail viewing distribution, and a separate live pipeline using RTMP/SRT ingest with LL-HLS or WebRTC depending on latency target** — the same architecture YouTube, Netflix, and Twitch run for video at scale.
